Watersprings
waw'ter-springs
n. pl. (natural springs of water; in Psalm 107 the emblem of God's power to reverse a land's fortunes either way)
From water and spring, rendering Hebrew motsa mayim, an outgoing or source of water. A spring in that country was not a convenience but the difference between a settlement and a desert.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs twice in one psalm, in two verses that are exact mirrors. First the drying: “He turneth rivers into a wilderness, and the watersprings into dry ground” (Psalm 107:33), and the reason is given in the next verse — “A fruitful land into barrenness, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein” (Psalm 107:34). Then the reverse: “He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings” (Psalm 107:35), and there too the sequel is given — “And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation” (Psalm 107:36). The same verb, the same God, opposite directions. The psalm has spent its earlier stanzas on four groups delivered from four distresses — the lost, the imprisoned, the sick and the storm-tossed — each with the refrain Oh that men would praise the LORD for his goodness. These two verses generalise the pattern to geography itself. Fertility and desolation are not simply the weather; they are the acts of the God who governs both, and the psalm ends by saying that whoso is wise will observe these things.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a spring as a fountain of water, an issue of water from the earth, and the source or head of a stream.

expand to see more

SPRING, n. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at the place of its issue.

2. The source of anything; that from which a thing proceeds.

WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.

BARRENNESS, n. The quality of not producing its kind; want of the power of conception; sterility.

HABITATION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode.

Key Scripture

Psalm 107:33 — "He turneth rivers into a wilderness, and the watersprings into dry ground;"

Psalm 107:35 — "He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings."

Psalm 107:34 — "A fruitful land into barrenness, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein."

Psalm 107:36 — "And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation;"

Modern Corruption

Land and weather are removed from providence altogether, or else read as a simple scorecard of a nation's righteousness.

expand to see more

Psalm 107:34 says a fruitful land is turned to barrenness for the wickedness of them that dwell therein, and there are two ways to get this wrong. The first is to deny that God has anything to do with the physical fortunes of a place, which the psalm plainly asserts that He does. The second, and the one more common among people who take the verse seriously, is to reverse it into a diagnostic tool — reading every drought and every disaster as a decoded message about a particular sin. Our Lord forbade exactly that inference about the tower of Siloam and the Galileans, and Job's comforters were rebuked for practising it. God governs the rain; He has not licensed anyone to publish the reasons.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's symmetry, which is a comfort more than a threat. The God who dries up the springs is the God who turns the wilderness into standing water, and He does the second for the hungry, so that they may prepare a city. The reversals run both directions and the second is the direction the psalm ends on. A congregation looking at a dry season — in a family, a ministry, a nation — is being told by verse 35 that the same hand which emptied the spring can open one in a desert, and by verse 43 that the wise will watch for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew motsa mayim, a spring or outgoing of water — Psalm 107:33, 107:35; midbar, wilderness; tsimmaon, thirsty ground.

expand to see more

Hebrew motsa — a going forth, a source; joined with mayim, water, for the springs of Psalm 107:33, 35.

Hebrew midbar — wilderness, uninhabited pasture land; the term the psalm moves in both directions.

Hebrew melechah — saltness, barrenness; Psalm 107:34, of the fruitful land turned.

Hebrew agam mayim — a pool or standing water; Psalm 107:35, the wilderness reversed.

Psalm 107:43 closes the psalm: whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD.

Usage

"“He turneth… the watersprings into dry ground” — and the reason follows in the next verse."

"“He turneth the wilderness into a standing water” — the same verb, the other direction."

"“There he maketh the hungry to dwell” — the reversal is for somebody."
